opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, my interest in reading conference papers has dropped quite a lot over the past few years, and it's mostly because of how I've come to see the problems people are working on.

When I was starting out in NLP, conference papers felt like the frontier. You'd read ACL or NeurIPS proceedings and get a real sense of where the field was going. Now, at least for the work I care about, which is large models and pushing their capabilities, a lot of the truly important problems simply can't be studied well at the scale most academic papers operate at. Many papers tune something on a small model or a narrow benchmark, get a point or two of improvement, and write it up. That's a legitimate way to do research, but often the conclusions don't hold once you scale up, or the problem disappears entirely with a stronger base model and better data.

So I've become more selective. I ask: is this problem still a problem at the frontier? Does the insight survive scaling? If the answer is probably not, I don't spend much time on it. I'd rather read a handful of solid technical reports, look closely at what different teams actually did with data, training recipes, and infrastructure, and then run experiments myself. In this area, a lot of the real knowledge sits in practice and engineering detail more than in the paper format.

I don't want to sound dismissive of academia, though. There's still very valuable work: new ideas in architecture, evaluation, theory, analysis of model behavior. Those can be really inspiring. It's just that the ratio of signal to noise has changed, and the questions I find most worth focusing on, like how to make models reason better or how to use compute more efficiently, are increasingly answered by doing rather than by reading. So my reading habits followed that shift.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts frontier-scale problems with work in academic papers, but it does not say that researchers with large-scale compute experience pursue problems that overlap little with those pursued by researchers without that experience.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I read far fewer conference papers now than I did when I was a PhD student. Back then, I treated every ACL or NeurIPS deadline as a kind of map of the field, and I felt anxious if I missed a batch. Now my feeling is that most papers are answering questions that were set by the structure of academia itself, not by what actually matters for building strong models.

What I mean is this. A paper has to be publishable in a few months, by a small team, on limited compute. So the problems people choose are shaped by those constraints. You get many incremental tricks, a new attention variant, a new loss, a few points of improvement on a benchmark at a scale where the conclusion may not hold anymore when you go ten or a hundred times larger. The result is that a lot of the literature is very clever but not very load-bearing. When you train at real scale, you discover that maybe eighty or ninety percent of those ideas simply wash out, and the things that remain are often the boring ones: data quality, scaling laws, training stability, infrastructure.

So my interest in reading has become much more selective. I still read, but I read with a specific question in mind. I ask, does this paper change my belief about something that matters at scale? Does it tell me something about where the limits are, rather than how to squeeze one more point? And I pay more attention to work that is honest about negative results, or that studies phenomena like emergence, memorization, or reasoning failures, because those tell me about the shape of the problem rather than about one more method.

I would also say that a lot of the most important knowledge in this field now is not in papers at all. It lives in training runs, in internal post-mortems, in the intuitions of people who have broken a big run and fixed it. Papers are lagging indicators. So for me, the shift is from reading papers to understand the frontier, to reading papers to check whether my own understanding, formed from practice, is missing something. That is a very different relationship to the literature, and I think it is a healthier one.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts research shaped by small-team, limited-compute constraints with lessons from training at real scale, but does not clearly state that the problems pursued by experienced large-compute teams overlap little with those pursued by researchers without that experience.

astra-6.text: For me, the question a paper asks matters more than how sophisticated the method is. If I feel the problem is worth solving, I’m very interested in reading it and understanding the authors’ approach. But if the motivation doesn’t convince me, it’s hard to get excited about an improvement on a benchmark. So my interest in conference papers depends a lot on whether researchers are working on questions that I find meaningful.

r001.rationale: The response says interest depends on whether a paper’s problem feels meaningful, but does not compare the problems pursued by researchers with and without large-scale compute team experience or say that they overlap little.

sol-6.1.text: I tend to ask whether the problem itself is worth solving before looking at how clever the method is. If a paper focuses on a narrow problem mainly because it fits an established benchmark, I find it harder to get interested. I’m more drawn to papers that identify a meaningful problem or challenge an assumption. So my interest in reading conference papers depends a lot on whether the questions researchers are asking feel important to me.

r001.rationale: The response discusses whether research problems seem important and benchmark-driven, but it does not compare the problems pursued by researchers with and without large-scale compute team experience.
